document.title: Mahmud Plans 2nd Mission to Afghanistan (Islamabad 05337)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), New Documents Detail America's Strategic Response to 9/11
document.note: [Secret] ISI Director Mahmoud tells Ambassador Chamberlin he will make a last-minute plea to the Taliban, preferring a negotiated solution and saying Omar is frightened. He promises full Pakistani support, including for military action. Chamberlin says Omar has refused every U.S. demand and the trip cannot delay military planning.

events.description: Mahmud met Mullah Omar; Omar was intransigent.
Planned second Mahmud trip to meet Omar, possibly with Pakistani religious leaders, to press for surrender of bin Laden and release of Shelter Now detainees.
Mahmud briefed Ambassador Chamberlin during JCS/CENTCOM military coordination discussions.
September 11 attacks; US ended willingness to negotiate with the Taliban.
Mahmud planned a second trip to Afghanistan as early as Sept 25 to meet Omar, possibly with Pakistani religious leaders.
JCS/CENTCOM team met Pakistani counterparts for joint military coordination; Mahmud briefed the Ambassador.
U.S. willingness to continue discussions with the Taliban ended after September 11.
Pakistan planned to withdraw its remaining diplomats from Afghanistan within 48 hours and was considering severing relations.

key_claims: ISI chief Mahmud planned a second mission to Mullah Omar to demand surrender of bin Laden and al-Qa'ida, closure and inspection of camps, and release of Shelter Now detainees.
Mahmud claimed the mission ran parallel to US-Pakistani military planning and did not change Pakistan's commitments.
Mahmud argued the Taliban were weak, Omar frightened, and that Afghans should deal with al-Qa'ida themselves.
Mahmud warned that eliminating the Taliban would produce warlordism and a generation of angry young Muslim men.
Pakistan planned to withdraw its remaining diplomats from Afghanistan within 48 hours and was considering severing relations as the UAE had.
The US Embassy assessed Mahmud had virtually no chance of success, but the mission served Musharraf's domestic political needs.
